props.headline: We Built the Database We Wished We Had
props.subheadline: TiDB started in 2015 with three infrastructure engineers and a problem they couldn't stop thinking about. This is the story of what they built, who it's for, and where it's going.

items.content:
In 2015, three infrastructure engineers were tired of how databases were managed at large internet companies. Every time an application grew, managing, scaling, and maintaining the database took far more effort than it should have.

They looked for a database that could grow with the application without that pain. They didn't find one. So they started building it, in the open, and named the company PingCAP.

That project became TiDB. Max Liu, one of the three, still leads the company as CEO. You can [watch him talk about the architecture behind it](https://youtu.be/g0OikEsHPV4).

image.alt: Max Liu, co-founder and CEO of PingCAP, speaking on stage
Max Liu, co-founder and CEO of PingCAP, speaking on stage

items.content:
Open source wasn't a decision we made later. TiDB was open from the first commit, and it still is. Hundreds of contributors around the world help build it, and TiKV, the storage engine underneath TiDB, is a graduated project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

Working in the open keeps us honest. Anyone can read the code, question a design choice, or fix something we missed. By the end of 2026, we plan to open source the core of TiDB X, our newest architecture, so the next version of TiDB is built the same way the first one was.

> "Open source is our gene. It's our DNA. It has been open for us since day one. As an engineer, I love open source."

Max Liu, co-founder and CEO

props.title: Built Alongside the People Who Run It

items.content:
The hardest problems we've worked on came from customers who wouldn't accept a limit. Atlassian runs Jira and Confluence for tens of millions of people on systems that can never go down. Pinterest, Plaid, Flipkart, and many others brought workloads their previous databases struggled to handle.

Each of them pushed TiDB further than we would have on our own. Ten years in, we still build it the same way: alongside the engineers who depend on it.

> "For our customers, this is not ephemeral data. This is their system of record. We do not tolerate any downtime."

Vinod Kumar, Atlassian, speaking at TiDB SCaiLE 2026

props.title: A New Kind of User, the Same Old Problem

items.content:
This year something new happened. Most of the databases created on TiDB Cloud weren't started by a person at all. They were started by AI agents, building apps on someone's behalf.

It's a different kind of user, but it's the problem we started with: the database shouldn't be what holds the work back.

Agents are temporary. Their work isn't. Behind every agent there is still a person who needs that work to be there tomorrow, and a team that needs it to be correct.

That's who we build for. Whether it's an enterprise running core systems or a startup shipping something new this week, it's the same database underneath.
